function by modulating local brain region excitability [11],
[12], [13], the execution of motor behavior relies on dynamic
interactions among multiple brain regions, thereby limiting
its therapeutic efﬁcacy [14], [15]. Dual-Target Brain Region
Stimulation is an emerging neurostimulation strategy that
sequentially stimulates multiple functionally complementary
brain regions, offering advantages in integrating dual-brain
region synergistic effects and optimizing neural signal trans-
mission pathways [16], [17], [18]. Importantly, sequential
dual-target TMS has demonstrated signiﬁcant therapeutic efﬁ-
cacy in conditions such as consciousness disorders, post-stroke
motor function recovery, and cognitive impairments [19], [20],
[21].
In neurostimulation strategies for promoting rehabilitation

of lower limb motor disorders, the supplementary motor
area (SMA) is a commonly used stimulation site for rTMS.
Research indicates that the SMA receives neural inputs from
multiple levels, including primary and secondary somatosen-
sory areas, the parietal association cortex, and projections
from the basal ganglia via the thalamus [22]. These connec-
tions form the basal ganglia-thalamus-cortex-SMA functional
circuit, which is involved in the autonomous generation of
internal movements, automated behaviors, and the planning
and initiation of learned motor sequences [23]. On the other
hand, the SMA sends projection ﬁbers to the corticospinal
tract. As shown in Fig. 1. Through this unique corticospinal
projection, the SMA not only participates in the planning
and initiation stages of movement but also directly intervenes
in the execution process of movement [24]. Notably, recent
studies have shown that the relationship between cognition
and movement is complementary rather than competitive [25].
The results of Yu et al. [26] also conﬁrm that rTMS treatment
of the left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (L-DLPFC) improves

patients’ balance and postural control abilities and signiﬁcantly
reduces the risk of falls in daily life. Additionally, previous
literature suggests that the L-DLPFC is responsible for plan-
ning, organizing, and regulating motor functions [27], [28]
and may maintain postural control and balance through the
allocation of attentional resources [29]. Another study suggests
that the frontal cortex indirectly inﬂuences basal neural circuits
through projections to the SMA [30]. Therefore, we hypothe-
size that stimulating the L-DLPFC ﬁrst may promote resource
integration within the cognitive-motor network, followed by
stimulation of the SMA to further regulate the immediate reor-
ganization of movement-related networks, thereby enhancing
neural plasticity across multiple brain regions. It should be
noted that “dual-target rTMS” in this study refers to sequential
stimulation of the L-DLPFC and the SMA. However, the
underlying mechanisms of this temporal network regulation
remain poorly understood.
Understanding the potential mechanisms underlying motor

recovery induced by different intervention modalities is cru-
cial for enhancing our understanding of neural mechanisms
and further optimizing motor rehabilitation strategies. Func-
tional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) is a neuroimaging
technique used to monitor cortical hemodynamics. Its mea-
surement principle is based on the optical properties of the
medium being studied, so near-infrared light signals are funda-
mentally less susceptible to electromagnetic interference from
TMS pulses and impose no restrictions on the placement of
TMS coils [31], [32]. These characteristics of fNIRS make
it well-suited for use in conjunction with TMS, enabling the
study of the immediate effects of TMS on brain functional
networks.
Traditional static functional connectivity analysis is based

on the assumption that functional interactions between differ-
ent brain regions remain static throughout the scan. However,
brain regions do not interact statically but rather through
dynamic processes [33], [34], [35]. Dynamic functional net-
work connectivity (dFNC) aids in studying dynamic functional
interactions between brain networks and better captures the
dynamic temporal properties of brain functional networks
during TMS stimulation. Therefore, in this study, we aimed
to investigate the effects of single-target and sequential dual-
target stimulation on brain functional networks in stroke
patients (Stroke) and healthy controls (HC) using dFNC anal-
ysis methods with fNIRS. We hypothesize that: (1) there are
signiﬁcant differences in the temporal characteristics of dFNC
between Stroke and HC; (2) changes in the temporal char-
acteristics of dFNC are associated with the severity of lower
limb motor impairments in stroke patients; (3) Compared to
single-target stimulation, sequential dual-target rTMS induces
more pronounced alterations in brain network dynamics.
This study recruited a total of 20 patients with subacute

stroke from the hospital afﬁliated with the National Research
Center for Rehabilitation Technical Aids. The inclusion cri-
teria were as follows: (1) radiological evidence of unilateral

subcortical stroke; (2) age between 20 and 85 years; (3)
the enrollment period was within 7 days and 6 months
after the onset of the disease; (4) presence of mild, mod-
erate, or severe unilateral lower limb motor dysfunction,
as deﬁned by the Fugl-Meyer Assessment for Lower Extrem-
ity (FMA-LE) with the following cutoff scores [36]: severe
(FMA-LE < 19), moderate (FMA-LE 20–28), and mild
(FMA-LE > 29) (5) no contraindications for rTMS mea-
surement; (6) ability to understand and follow instructions.
During the course of this study, three subjects were excluded
due to poor compliance, as they were unable to complete
data collection in accordance with the study requirements.
Additionally, two subjects were excluded after fNIRS data
preprocessing due to excessive motion artifacts resulting in
low signal-to-noise ratios, which did not meet the quality
requirements for fNIRS data analysis. After rigorous data
veriﬁcation, a total of 15 stroke patients were ultimately
included for subsequent analysis. Additionally, 15 healthy
participants matched for age, gender, and educational level,
with no history of mental or neurological disorders, were
recruited as controls. All patients underwent a series of clinical
assessments, including National Institutes of Health Stroke
Scale (NIHSS), Fugl-Meyer Lower Limb Motor Function
Assessment Scale (FMA-LE), Berg Balance Scale (BBS), and
Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE). Table I describes
the detailed demographic data and clinical characteristics of
the participants, including age, gender, time since stroke onset,
and cognitive status. According to the Chinese version of the
Dominant Hand Scale [37], all participants were right-handed.
All patients signed informed consent forms and were informed
of potential adverse events prior to the trial. This study (Trial
Registration: ChiCTR2000035984) was approved by Ethics
Committee of Yueyang Integrative Medicine Hospital afﬁliated
to Shanghai University of Traditional Chinese Medicine and
strictly adheres to the ethical standards for medical research as
stipulated in the 1975 Helsinki Declaration (revised in 2008).
This study is a randomized, prospective, cross-sectional

clinical trial. All participants must complete three experimental
sessions under different intervention conditions, with each
session spaced more than 48 hours apart [38], [39]. The exper-
imental intervention conditions include: (1) SMA single target
stimulation (SMA-rTMS), (2) L-DLPFC single target stimu-
lation (LDLPFC-rTMS), (3) Sequential dual-target rTMS of
the L-DLPFC and SMA (Dual-rTMS). The order of the three
experimental sessions was assigned using a random sequence
generated by MATLAB (The MathWorks, Inc., Natick, MA,
USA) and balanced across participants. Each experimental ses-
sion consisted of two stages: a 6-minute resting-state recording
and a 10-minute transcranial magnetic stimulation interven-
tion. Prior to the experiment, participants were instructed
to rest in a quiet environment for 10-20 minutes to relax
both mentally and physically. Subsequently, fNIRS was used
to simultaneously detect dynamic hemodynamic information
during resting state and rTMS. Additionally, participants were
required to remain awake and avoid voluntary movements and

speech during both the resting state and transcranial magnetic
stimulation.
The TMS used in this study was a magnetic ﬁeld stimulator

with a cone-shaped coil(Yiruide MagTD, Wuhan, China).
For healthy subjects, the resting motor threshold (rMT) was
measured over the right primary motor cortex (M1). The
rMT was deﬁned as the minimum stimulus intensity required
to elicit motor evoked potentials with an amplitude greater
than 50 μV in at least 5 out of 10 stimuli recorded from
the contralateral abductor pollicis brevis muscle. For patients,
if the above method fails to obtain rMT from the affected
side M1, the location of the healthy hemisphere M1 is deﬁned
as the stimulation target, and the healthy hemisphere rMT
is used as the intervention intensity for rTMS. Fig. 2 shows
the intervention parameters for different experimental phases,
as follows: SMA-rTMS: 10 Hz, 100% rMT, 1000 pulses (2
s × 50 trains, 10 s interval); LDLPFC-rTMS: 10 Hz, 80%
rMT, 1000 pulses (5 s × 20 trains, 25 s interval); Dual-rTMS:
5 minutes of LDLPFC-rTMS followed by 5 minutes of SMA-
rTMS, totaling 1000 pulses. Additionally, the stimulation site
for L-DLPFC was located at F3 using the ﬁber cap positioning
from the international 10/20 EEG system [40], and the SMA
stimulation point was deﬁned as the scalp location 3 cm
anterior to the CZ point [41], [42]. All stimulation was admin-
istered by an experienced neurologist who was not involved
in the clinical assessment or data analysis of the participants.
Brain hemodynamic responses during resting state and TMS

intervention were collected using a multi-channel continuous
wave (740 nm and 850 nm) fNIRS device (NirSmart, Danyang
Huichuang Medical Equipment Co., LTD., Beijing, China)
in a quiet environment. The data sampling frequency was
set to 10 Hz. Following the international 10-20 system [43],
16 detector probes and 18 light source probes were symmetri-
cally arranged on both sides of the prefrontal cortex and motor
cortex, forming a total of 38 signal channels, with a channel
spacing of 30 mm. To achieve precise localization of channel
signals within brain regions, we acquired three-dimensional
coordinates for all probes and key anatomical landmarks
such as the nasal root and preauricular point using a 3D
digitizer. These coordinates were then mapped to the Montreal
Neurological Institute standard space [44]. Subsequently, prob-
abilistic mapping analysis was performed using NIRS-SPM
software [45]. Signals were categorized into 14 regions of
interest based on Brodmann areas: bilateral prefrontal cortex
(PFC), dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC), superior frontal
cortex (SFC), presupplementary motor area (PSMA), M1,
primary somatosensory cortex (S1), and occipital cortex (OC).
Additionally, to ensure compatibility with TMS equipment,
a TMS-speciﬁc probe was employed to mitigate limitations
such as shallow TMS penetration depth and susceptibility to
interference.

The K-means clustering algorithm was applied to identify

recurrent FC patterns across all subjects and time windows.
Notably, the cluster analysis was performed based on the
dFNC data from all subjects across all experimental condi-
tions. Prior to clustering, each L×L FC matrix derived from
sliding time windows was transformed into a feature vector
representing dFNC. Speciﬁcally, the upper triangular ele-
ments (excluding the diagonal) of each matrix were extracted
and reshaped into one-dimensional vectors of length L×(L–
1)/2, hereafter termed dFNC vectors. Manhattan distance was
employed to quantify similarity between these dFNC vectors.
To avoid getting stuck in local optima, the maximum number
of iterations was set to 500, and the number of repetitions
was set to 150 [53]. Additionally, the elbow method was used
to determine the optimal number of states as 3. Finally, two
dFNC metrics were calculated: (1) the fraction time (FT),
deﬁned as the ratio of the number of time windows in a
state to the total number of time windows, and (2) the state
transition percentage (STP), which describes the likelihood of
transitioning from one state to another.

To investigate energy consumption patterns across different

brain states, we employed the Welch algorithm to compute the
power spectral density (PSD) of HbO2. A Hanning window
with a length of 200 data points and 50% overlap was
applied. After calculating the PSD for each window, numerical

The Kolmogorov-Smirnov test and Levene’s test were used

to assess the variance, normality, and homogeneity of the data
at the group level. A two-sample t-test was employed to detect
group differences in normally distributed data, while the non-
parametric Mann-Whitney U test was used for non-normally
distributed data. Group differences included scores related to
age, gender, MMSE, NIHSS, FMA-LE, and BBS. To exam-
ine the effects on dFNC temporal characteristics, a series
of two-way mixed ANOVAs were conducted with Health
Status (HC vs. Stroke) as a between-subjects factor and Inter-
vention Mode (Resting-state, SMA-rTMS, LDLPFC-rTMS,
Dual-rTMS) as a within-subjects factor. These analyses were
performed separately for the FT of each dFNC state. Post-hoc
comparisons with Bonferroni correction were applied when
signiﬁcant main or interaction effects were found. Finally,
Spearman’s rank correlation analysis was used to explore
the relationship between dFNC temporal characteristics and
clinical variables. Statistical signiﬁcance was set at P < 0.05.
All statistical analyses were performed using SPSS version
25.0 software.

Recent studies have effectively demonstrated the tempo-

ral variability of intrinsic brain networks, indicating that
functional connectivity in the human brain is indeed highly
dynamic, reﬂecting the ﬂexibility of functional coordination
between different brain systems [56], [57]. Consistent with the
results of previous reports, this study identiﬁed three recurrent
dFNC states, with State 1 occupying the largest number
of total time windows. Compared to the other two states,
State 1 exhibits a “sparse connectivity state” characterized

by weak connections and low integration, a ﬁnding consistent
with previous studies in patients with schizophrenia, diabetes,
and stroke [50], [55], [56]. This weak connectivity reﬂects
the brain’s baseline connectivity pattern and suggests that
the human brain may tend to maintain this low-efﬁciency
information transmission state to conserve energy [58], [59].
However, we observed a negative correlation between the
FT spent in state 1 during baseline resting conditions in
Stroke and motor function scores. This suggests that the
persistent dominance of this state in pathological contexts
more likely reﬂects impaired network integration capacity.
This ﬁnding aligns with evidence showing that prolonged
dwell time in weak-connectivity states after stroke correlates
with impaired neurological recovery [58], [60]. State 3 exhibits
stronger regional and hemispheric connectivity, consistent with
the characteristics of a “highly integrated state,” but it has
the lowest time proportion (16.32%), potentially reﬂecting
the brain’s efﬁcient information processing capacity within a
limited timeframe.
To more speciﬁcally characterize the connectivity features

of each state, the GE of each state was also calculated.
From the GE perspective, the results of this study align
with ﬁndings from a Parkinson’s disease study indicating
that “higher connectivity states correspond to higher global
efﬁciency” [51]. This suggests that the dynamic layering of
brain networks may follow an “efﬁciency-stability” trade-off
principle, where the high connectivity of State 3 supports
rapid information transmission but comes with higher energy
consumption; the low connectivity of State 1 reduces energy
consumption but may impair cross-regional collaboration. The
differences in this layering across different intervention modes
provide functional-level evidence for understanding brain net-
work reorganization in disease states.
This study also found that, regardless of whether it was

the HC group or the Stroke group, Dual-rTMS signiﬁcantly
increased the FT of State 1 and to some extent reduced the
FT of State 2 and State 3.This phenomenon may suggest
that Dual-rTMS induces a shift in the brain toward a low-

Research indicates that while intracranial stimulation ini-

tially causes a temporary reduction in the brain network’s
switching capacity and synchrony, this trend gradually stabi-
lizes over time [61]. Intergroup comparisons revealed that the
STP for the transition from State 2 to State 3 was signiﬁcantly
lower in the Stroke group than in the healthy control group.
This indicates impaired ability for the post-stroke brain to
transition from a moderately integrated state to a highly inte-
grated, efﬁcient state. Integrating these ﬁndings, we propose
that this rTMS-induced increase in State 1 FT may repre-
sent a distinct neural mechanism. Speciﬁcally, Dual-rTMS
signiﬁcantly reduced the STP from State 1 to State 2. The
combination of increased State 1 FT and reduced transition
probability suggests that rTMS may actively impose a network
stabilization or reset by disrupting brain network communi-

cation mechanisms. This temporarily suppresses inefﬁcient,
maladaptive ﬂuctuations, enabling the brain to stably maintain
the low-energy State 1, thereby creating an opportunity for
subsequent functional reorganization.
Therefore, this study speculates that sequential dual-target

stimulation may exert a dual regulatory effect on neural
mechanisms: on one hand, by inhibiting the transition from
State 1 to State 2, it reduces inefﬁcient network ﬂuctuations;
on the other hand, the trend toward reduced FT in State
3 may prevent excessive energy consumption and maintain
network homeostasis. This dynamic balance may explain
why sequential dual-target intervention outperforms single-
target stimulation in improving outcomes for lower-limb stroke
patients, as it optimizes the functional coupling efﬁciency
of motor-related brain regions by regulating the temporal
distribution and transition probabilities of network states.
This study revealed unique characteristics of functional

network dynamics in Stroke. Compared with healthy controls,
the Stroke group exhibited a reduction in STP from State
2 to State 3, reﬂecting impaired ability to transition to a state
of strong hemispheric connectivity. Similarly, many studies
have shown that reduced interhemispheric connectivity is a
core feature of stroke [62], [63]. Siegel et al. [64] previously
proposed that increased modularity is associated with post-
stroke recovery. Our results further suggest that not only the
degree of modularity itself but also the dynamic transition
ability between states may be key indicators of functional
prognosis. Interestingly, while bilateral stimulation primarily
affects State 1 in HC group, it also signiﬁcantly impacts the FT
of State 2 in the Stroke group, a difference that may reﬂect the
Stroke brain’s speciﬁc response pattern to neuromodulation.
Additionally, our correlation analysis results showed that the
FT of State 1 in the Stroke group was negatively correlated
with lower limb motor function scores and balance function,
while the FT of State 3 was positively correlated with lower
limb motor function scores and balance function, providing
potential neuroimaging markers for clinical assessment.
The pathological oscillations occurring within the network

may trigger the symptoms induced by the stroke, and stimula-
tion of any node within the neural network could disrupt this
pathological rhythm [65]. We propose that the interpretation of
State 1 exhibits dual characteristics: Speciﬁcally, under patho-
logical conditions, the persistent dominance of State 1 indeed
reﬂects a loss of network integration capacity. Conversely,
we suggest that rTMS (particularly dual-target stimulation) can
disrupt the dynamic rhythms of brain networks, transforming
the current state into a controllable stable state. It is con-
ceivable that establishing new connections from this weakly
connected state may be more feasible, laying the groundwork
for greater network ﬂexibility [66].
It is important to note that the neural effects of the temporal

stimulation paradigm employed in this study are complex.
A key consideration is the potential inﬂuence of homeo-
static plasticity. Homeostatic plasticity mechanisms ensure
neuronal network excitability remains within physiological

bounds, with the history of prior synaptic activity modulating
the direction and extent of plasticity induced by subsequent
stimulation [67], [68]. In this study, the initial high-frequency
rTMS applied to the L-DLPFC may have induced height-

ened excitability in this region and its associated networks.
Given the functional and anatomical connectivity between the
DLPFC and SMA, this alteration may have correspondingly
modiﬁed the baseline excitability state of the SMA prior

to receiving stimulation. Consequently, the effects of the
subsequent rTMS applied to the SMA may not represent a
simple superposition but rather an optimized network response
pattern, regulated by homeostatic plasticity, that differs from
what would be observed with single-target stimulation alone.

Dual-target
neuromodulation
therapy
is
an
emerging

research direction in neuroscience [69]. A meta-analysis of
22 studies showed that compared to single-target stimula-
tion, sequential dual-target stimulation can achieve higher
efﬁcacy by enhancing neural network plasticity and improv-
ing functional connectivity across cognitive domains [16].
Additionally, high-frequency rTMS (HF-rTMS) applied in a
sequential dual-target stimulation paradigm has been shown to
enhance synaptic efﬁcacy, induce effects similar to long-term
potentiation, and strengthen functional connectivity between
brain regions [70], [71]. Similarly, in this study, HF-rTMS
was sequentially applied to the L-DLPFC and SMA of Stroke
with lower limb motor dysfunction, and it was found that the
connectivity between M1_L, S1_L, and DLPFC_R, SFC_R
varied to different degrees within different dFNC states. This
suggests that the current study protocol may better reshape the
nervous system by optimizing the cross-regional information
integration patterns between the frontal-sensorimotor cortex-
motor cortex loop in patients. The aforementioned mechanisms
and results suggest that rTMS methods based on neural net-
work regulation may promote brain functional remodeling in
Stroke by enhancing synaptic plasticity and repairing damaged
functional connections.
In summary, our study further validates that the therapeu-

tic mechanisms of rTMS can inﬂuence dynamic functional
connectivity between large-scale brain networks. Addition-
ally, dynamic functional connectivity between brain networks
can serve as a predictive indicator of rTMS treatment efﬁ-
cacy. Finally, for Stroke with lower limb motor impairments,
compared to traditional single-target stimulation, sequential
dual-target stimulation may represent an efﬁcient therapeutic
modality to promote brain remodeling.
Our study also has some limitations. First, a potential limita-

tion of this study is the absence of a sham-rTMS control group.
Future experimental designs should include a sham-rTMS
group as a control to better understand the effects of different
stimulation patterns on dynamic brain functional networks.
Second, the selection of sliding window size may inﬂuence
the assessment of dynamic brain connectivity. Future analyses
should be conducted using different window widths to validate
the reliability and reproducibility of the results. Third, the 48-
hour washout period may have been too short to completely
avoid carryover effects between experimental sessions. Fourth,
the localization of stimulation targets (L-DLPFC and SMA)
in this study relied on EEG caps based on the international
10-20 system rather than individualized MRI navigation. This
may introduce some degree of inter-individual variability.
Future studies employing individualized neuro-navigation will
enhance the precision of target localization. Finally, a key
limitation of this study is the absence of resting-state fNIRS
measurements following rTMS intervention. Consequently,
our ﬁndings capture only the immediate online effects of
stimulation, without clarifying whether the observed dynamic
functional network connectivity changes (e.g., increased FT
in state 1) persist as a lasting aftereffect into the post-
stimulation phase. Future studies should incorporate longer
post-intervention monitoring periods to elucidate the temporal
dynamics and potential enduring beneﬁts of sequential dual-
target TMS.

INTRODUCTION
STROKE is a common clinical cerebrovascular disease with high incidence, mortality, and disability rates. It is mainly

caused by cerebral vascular rupture or embolism, leading to ischemia and hypoxia in brain tissue, which in turn causes nerve cell death and seriously affects the health and life of patients [1], [2]. After a stroke, patients often experience various neurological sequelae, with hemiplegia being a common sequela that leads to balance dysfunction and impaired walking ability. According to reports, nearly 80% of stroke patients are unable to successfully maintain balance and control their walking posture [3]. Previous studies have shown that the neurobiological basis for motor function recovery after stroke lies in the plasticity of the central nervous system [4], [5]. During this process, the central nervous system reorganizes its structure and function to reestablish neural connections, thereby partially compensating for the functional impairments caused by damage to the lesion area [6], [7]. Therefore, promoting and restoring neural plasticity is a key intervention strategy in the motor rehabilitation of stroke patients.

This work involved human subjects or animals in its research. While traditional single-target TMS can improve motor function by modulating local brain region excitability [11], [12], [13], the execution of motor behavior relies on dynamic interactions among multiple brain regions, thereby limiting its therapeutic efﬁcacy [14], [15]. Dual-Target Brain Region Stimulation is an emerging neurostimulation strategy that sequentially stimulates multiple functionally complementary brain regions, offering advantages in integrating dual-brain region synergistic effects and optimizing neural signal transmission pathways [16], [17], [18]. Importantly, sequential dual-target TMS has demonstrated signiﬁcant therapeutic efﬁcacy in conditions such as consciousness disorders, post-stroke motor function recovery, and cognitive impairments [19], [20], [21].

In neurostimulation strategies for promoting rehabilitationof lower limb motor disorders, the supplementary motor area (SMA) is a commonly used stimulation site for rTMS. Research indicates that the SMA receives neural inputs from multiple levels, including primary and secondary somatosensory areas, the parietal association cortex, and projections from the basal ganglia via the thalamus [22]. These connections form the basal ganglia-thalamus-cortex-SMA functional circuit, which is involved in the autonomous generation of internal movements, automated behaviors, and the planning and initiation of learned motor sequences [23]. On the other hand, the SMA sends projection ﬁbers to the corticospinal tract. As shown in Fig. 1. Through this unique corticospinal projection, the SMA not only participates in the planning and initiation stages of movement but also directly intervenes in the execution process of movement [24]. Notably, recent studies have shown that the relationship between cognition and movement is complementary rather than competitive [25]. The results of Yu et al. [26] also conﬁrm that rTMS treatment of the left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (L-DLPFC) improvespatients’ balance and postural control abilities and signiﬁcantly reduces the risk of falls in daily life. Additionally, previous literature suggests that the L-DLPFC is responsible for planning, organizing, and regulating motor functions [27], [28] and may maintain postural control and balance through the allocation of attentional resources [29]. Another study suggests that the frontal cortex indirectly inﬂuences basal neural circuits through projections to the SMA [30]. Therefore, we hypothesize that stimulating the L-DLPFC ﬁrst may promote resource integration within the cognitive-motor network, followed by stimulation of the SMA to further regulate the immediate reorganization of movement-related networks, thereby enhancing neural plasticity across multiple brain regions. It should be noted that “dual-target rTMS” in this study refers to sequential stimulation of the L-DLPFC and the SMA. However, the underlying mechanisms of this temporal network regulation remain poorly understood.

Understanding the potential mechanisms underlying motorrecovery induced by different intervention modalities is crucial for enhancing our understanding of neural mechanisms and further optimizing motor rehabilitation strategies. Functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) is a neuroimaging technique used to monitor cortical hemodynamics. Its measurement principle is based on the optical properties of the medium being studied, so near-infrared light signals are fundamentally less susceptible to electromagnetic interference from TMS pulses and impose no restrictions on the placement of TMS coils [31], [32]. These characteristics of fNIRS make it well-suited for use in conjunction with TMS, enabling the study of the immediate effects of TMS on brain functional networks.

Traditional static functional connectivity analysis is basedon the assumption that functional interactions between different brain regions remain static throughout the scan. However, brain regions do not interact statically but rather through dynamic processes [33], [34], [35]. Dynamic functional network connectivity (dFNC) aids in studying dynamic functional interactions between brain networks and better captures the dynamic temporal properties of brain functional networks during TMS stimulation. Therefore, in this study, we aimed to investigate the effects of single-target and sequential dualtarget stimulation on brain functional networks in stroke patients (Stroke) and healthy controls (HC) using dFNC analysis methods with fNIRS. We hypothesize that: (1) there are signiﬁcant differences in the temporal characteristics of dFNC between Stroke and HC; (2) changes in the temporal characteristics of dFNC are associated with the severity of lower limb motor impairments in stroke patients; (3) Compared to single-target stimulation, sequential dual-target rTMS induces more pronounced alterations in brain network dynamics.

MATERIALS AND METHODS
Participants

This study recruited a total of 20 patients with subacutestroke from the hospital afﬁliated with the National Research Center for Rehabilitation Technical Aids. The inclusion criteria were as follows: (1) radiological evidence of unilateral

subcortical stroke; (2) age between 20 and 85 years; (3) the enrollment period was within 7 days and 6 months after the onset of the disease; (4) presence of mild, moderate, or severe unilateral lower limb motor dysfunction, as deﬁned by the Fugl-Meyer Assessment for Lower Extremity (FMA-LE) with the following cutoff scores [36]: severe (FMA-LE < 19), moderate (FMA-LE 20–28), and mild (FMA-LE > 29) (5) no contraindications for rTMS measurement; (6) ability to understand and follow instructions. During the course of this study, three subjects were excluded due to poor compliance, as they were unable to complete data collection in accordance with the study requirements. Additionally, two subjects were excluded after fNIRS data preprocessing due to excessive motion artifacts resulting in low signal-to-noise ratios, which did not meet the quality requirements for fNIRS data analysis. After rigorous data veriﬁcation, a total of 15 stroke patients were ultimately included for subsequent analysis. Additionally, 15 healthy participants matched for age, gender, and educational level, with no history of mental or neurological disorders, were recruited as controls. All patients underwent a series of clinical assessments, including National Institutes of Health Stroke Scale (NIHSS), Fugl-Meyer Lower Limb Motor Function Assessment Scale (FMA-LE), Berg Balance Scale (BBS), and Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE). Table I describes the detailed demographic data and clinical characteristics of the participants, including age, gender, time since stroke onset, and cognitive status. According to the Chinese version of the Dominant Hand Scale [37], all participants were right-handed. All patients signed informed consent forms and were informed of potential adverse events prior to the trial. This study (Trial Registration: ChiCTR2000035984) was approved by Ethics Committee of Yueyang Integrative Medicine Hospital afﬁliated to Shanghai University of Traditional Chinese Medicine and strictly adheres to the ethical standards for medical research as stipulated in the 1975 Helsinki Declaration (revised in 2008).

Experimental Design and Procedures

This study is a randomized, prospective, cross-sectionalclinical trial. All participants must complete three experimental sessions under different intervention conditions, with each session spaced more than 48 hours apart [38], [39]. The experimental intervention conditions include: (1) SMA single target stimulation (SMA-rTMS), (2) L-DLPFC single target stimulation (LDLPFC-rTMS), (3) Sequential dual-target rTMS of the L-DLPFC and SMA (Dual-rTMS). The order of the three experimental sessions was assigned using a random sequence generated by MATLAB (The MathWorks, Inc., Natick, MA, USA) and balanced across participants. Each experimental session consisted of two stages: a 6-minute resting-state recording and a 10-minute transcranial magnetic stimulation intervention. Prior to the experiment, participants were instructed to rest in a quiet environment for 10-20 minutes to relax both mentally and physically. Subsequently, fNIRS was used to simultaneously detect dynamic hemodynamic information during resting state and rTMS. Additionally, participants were required to remain awake and avoid voluntary movements andspeech during both the resting state and transcranial magnetic stimulation.

The TMS used in this study was a magnetic ﬁeld stimulatorwith a cone-shaped coil(Yiruide MagTD, Wuhan, China). For healthy subjects, the resting motor threshold (rMT) was measured over the right primary motor cortex (M1). The rMT was deﬁned as the minimum stimulus intensity required to elicit motor evoked potentials with an amplitude greater than 50

V in at least 5 out of 10 stimuli recorded from the contralateral abductor pollicis brevis muscle. For patients, if the above method fails to obtain rMT from the affected side M1, the location of the healthy hemisphere M1 is deﬁned as the stimulation target, and the healthy hemisphere rMT is used as the intervention intensity for rTMS. Fig. 2 shows the intervention parameters for different experimental phases, as follows: SMA-rTMS: 10 Hz, 100% rMT, 1000 pulses (2 s × 50 trains, 10 s interval); LDLPFC-rTMS: 10 Hz, 80% rMT, 1000 pulses (5 s × 20 trains, 25 s interval); Dual-rTMS: 5 minutes of LDLPFC-rTMS followed by 5 minutes of SMArTMS, totaling 1000 pulses. Additionally, the stimulation site for L-DLPFC was located at F3 using the ﬁber cap positioning from the international 10/20 EEG system [40], and the SMA stimulation point was deﬁned as the scalp location 3 cm anterior to the CZ point [41], [42]. All stimulation was administered by an experienced neurologist who was not involved in the clinical assessment or data analysis of the participants.

fNIRS Measurement and Preprocessing

Brain hemodynamic responses during resting state and TMS intervention were collected using a multi-channel continuous wave (740 nm and 850 nm) fNIRS device (NirSmart, Danyang Huichuang Medical Equipment Co., LTD., Beijing, China) in a quiet environment. The data sampling frequency was set to 10 Hz. Following the international 10-20 system [43], 16 detector probes and 18 light source probes were symmetrically arranged on both sides of the prefrontal cortex and motor cortex, forming a total of 38 signal channels, with a channel spacing of 30 mm. To achieve precise localization of channel signals within brain regions, we acquired three-dimensional coordinates for all probes and key anatomical landmarks such as the nasal root and preauricular point using a 3D digitizer. These coordinates were then mapped to the Montreal Neurological Institute standard space [44]. Subsequently, probabilistic mapping analysis was performed using NIRS-SPM software [45]. Signals were categorized into 14 regions of interest based on Brodmann areas: bilateral prefrontal cortex (PFC), dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC), superior frontal cortex (SFC), presupplementary motor area (PSMA), M1, primary somatosensory cortex (S1), and occipital cortex (OC). Additionally, to ensure compatibility with TMS equipment, a TMS-speciﬁc probe was employed to mitigate limitations such as shallow TMS penetration depth and susceptibility to interference.

The K-means clustering algorithm was applied to identifyrecurrent FC patterns across all subjects and time windows. Notably, the cluster analysis was performed based on the dFNC data from all subjects across all experimental conditions. Prior to clustering, each L×L FC matrix derived from sliding time windows was transformed into a feature vector representing dFNC. Speciﬁcally, the upper triangular elements (excluding the diagonal) of each matrix were extracted and reshaped into one-dimensional vectors of length L×(L– 1)/2, hereafter termed dFNC vectors. Manhattan distance was employed to quantify similarity between these dFNC vectors. To avoid getting stuck in local optima, the maximum number of iterations was set to 500, and the number of repetitions was set to 150 [53]. Additionally, the elbow method was used to determine the optimal number of states as 3. Finally, two dFNC metrics were calculated: (1) the fraction time (FT), deﬁned as the ratio of the number of time windows in a state to the total number of time windows, and (2) the state transition percentage (STP), which describes the likelihood of transitioning from one state to another.

The K-means clustering algorithm was applied to identifyrecurrent FC patterns across all subjects and time windows. Notably, the cluster analysis was performed based on the dFNC data from all subjects across all experimental conditions. Prior to clustering, each L×L FC matrix derived from sliding time windows was transformed into a feature vector representing dFNC. Statistical Analysis

The Kolmogorov-Smirnov test and Levene’s test were usedto assess the variance, normality, and homogeneity of the data at the group level. A two-sample t-test was employed to detect group differences in normally distributed data, while the nonparametric Mann-Whitney U test was used for non-normally distributed data. Group differences included scores related to age, gender, MMSE, NIHSS, FMA-LE, and BBS. To examine the effects on dFNC temporal characteristics, a series of two-way mixed ANOVAs were conducted with Health Status (HC vs. Stroke) as a between-subjects factor and Intervention Mode (Resting-state, SMA-rTMS, LDLPFC-rTMS, Dual-rTMS) as a within-subjects factor. These analyses were performed separately for the FT of each dFNC state. Post-hoc comparisons with Bonferroni correction were applied when signiﬁcant main or interaction effects were found. Finally, Spearman’s rank correlation analysis was used to explore the relationship between dFNC temporal characteristics and clinical variables. Statistical signiﬁcance was set at P < 0.05. All statistical analyses were performed using SPSS version 25.0 software.

DISCUSSION

The human brain is essentially a complex system organized into a network, and this structure endows it with high ﬂexibility and enables it to function as a dynamic system as a whole [55].Therefore, it is necessary to study the effects of TMS on the brain from a dynamic perspective. Based on this, we used the dFNC method to investigate

the potential mechanisms underlying brain functional network remodeling under different rTMS intervention patterns. In this study, the K-means clustering algorithm was used to identify three relatively stable and recurrent connection states, these states exhibit distinct neurological characteristics: State 3 demonstrates the highest GE and total power, representing an integrated, high-energy-consumption pattern; State 1 exhibits the lowest GE and power, reﬂecting a low-connectivity, lowenergy-consumption pattern; State 2 presents intermediate features. Furthermore, rTMS modulated the temporal dynamics of these states: Dual-rTMS signiﬁcantly increased FT of state 1 while reducing its STP. The study also revealed key group differences: compared to HC, Stroke exhibited signiﬁcantly reduced STP from state 2 to state 3. Additionally, the

temporal characteristics of dFNC were signiﬁcantly correlated with patient questionnaire scores. The ﬁndings of this study provide new insights into the mechanisms underlying the effects of sequential dual-target TMS.

elements.value: Recent studies have effectively demonstrated the temporal variability of intrinsic brain networks, indicating that functional connectivity in the human brain is indeed highly dynamic, reﬂecting the ﬂexibility of functional coordination between different brain systems [56], [57]. Consistent with the results of previous reports, this study identiﬁed three recurrent dFNC states, with State 1 occupying the largest number of total time windows. Compared to the other two states, State 1 exhibits a “sparse connectivity state” characterized
8 IEEE TRANSACTIONS ON NEURAL SYSTEMS AND REHABILITATION ENGINEERING

by weak connections and low integration, a ﬁnding consistent with previous studies in patients with schizophrenia, diabetes, and stroke [50], [55], [56]. This weak connectivity reﬂects the brain’s baseline connectivity pattern and suggests that the human brain may tend to maintain this low-efﬁciency information transmission state to conserve energy [58], [59]. However, we observed a negative correlation between the FT spent in state 1 during baseline resting conditions in Stroke and motor function scores. This suggests that the persistent dominance of this state in pathological contexts more likely reﬂects impaired network integration capacity. This ﬁnding aligns with evidence showing that prolonged dwell time in weak-connectivity states after stroke correlates with impaired neurological recovery [58], [60]. State 3 exhibits stronger regional and hemispheric connectivity, consistent with the characteristics of a “highly integrated state,” but it has the lowest time proportion (16.32%), potentially reﬂecting the brain’s efﬁcient information processing capacity within a limited timeframe.

To more speciﬁcally characterize the connectivity featuresof each state, the GE of each state was also calculated. From the GE perspective, the results of this study align with ﬁndings from a Parkinson’s disease study indicating that “higher connectivity states correspond to higher global efﬁciency” [51]. This suggests that the dynamic layering of brain networks may follow an “efﬁciency-stability” trade-off principle, where the high connectivity of State 3 supports rapid information transmission but comes with higher energy consumption; the low connectivity of State 1 reduces energy consumption but may impair cross-regional collaboration. The differences in this layering across different intervention modes provide functional-level evidence for understanding brain network reorganization in disease states.

This study also found that, regardless of whether it wasthe HC group or the Stroke group, Dual-rTMS signiﬁcantly increased the FT of State 1 and to some extent reduced the FT of State 2 and State 3.This phenomenon may suggest that Dual-rTMS induces a shift in the brain toward a lowenergy state. Additionally, STP results showed that different stimulation patterns all exhibited signiﬁcant differences from the resting state to some extent, with Dual-rTMS causing a signiﬁcant reduction in STP for the transition from State 1 to State 2 in both the healthy group and the Stroke group.

Research indicates that while intracranial stimulation initially causes a temporary reduction in the brain network’s switching capacity and synchrony, this trend gradually stabilizes over time [61]. Intergroup comparisons revealed that the STP for the transition from State 2 to State 3 was signiﬁcantly lower in the Stroke group than in the healthy control group. This indicates impaired ability for the post-stroke brain to transition from a moderately integrated state to a highly integrated, efﬁcient state. Integrating these ﬁndings, we propose that this rTMS-induced increase in State 1 FT may represent a distinct neural mechanism. Speciﬁcally, Dual-rTMS signiﬁcantly reduced the STP from State 1 to State 2. The combination of increased State 1 FT and reduced transition probability suggests that rTMS may actively impose a network stabilization or reset by disrupting brain network communication mechanisms. This temporarily suppresses inefﬁcient, maladaptive ﬂuctuations, enabling the brain to stably maintain the low-energy State 1, thereby creating an opportunity for subsequent functional reorganization.

Therefore, this study speculates that sequential dual-targetstimulation may exert a dual regulatory effect on neural mechanisms: on one hand, by inhibiting the transition from State 1 to State 2, it reduces inefﬁcient network ﬂuctuations; on the other hand, the trend toward reduced FT in State 3 may prevent excessive energy consumption and maintain network homeostasis. This dynamic balance may explain why sequential dual-target intervention outperforms singletarget stimulation in improving outcomes for lower-limb stroke patients, as it optimizes the functional coupling efﬁciency of motor-related brain regions by regulating the temporal distribution and transition probabilities of network states.

Network Reorganization Mechanisms in Stroke

This study revealed unique characteristics of functionalnetwork dynamics in Stroke. Compared with healthy controls, the Stroke group exhibited a reduction in STP from State 2 to State 3, reﬂecting impaired ability to transition to a state of strong hemispheric connectivity. Similarly, many studies have shown that reduced interhemispheric connectivity is a core feature of stroke [62], [63]. Siegel et al. [64] previously proposed that increased modularity is associated with poststroke recovery. Our results further suggest that not only the degree of modularity itself but also the dynamic transition ability between states may be key indicators of functional prognosis. Interestingly, while bilateral stimulation primarily affects State 1 in HC group, it also signiﬁcantly impacts the FT of State 2 in the Stroke group, a difference that may reﬂect the Stroke brain’s speciﬁc response pattern to neuromodulation. Additionally, our correlation analysis results showed that the FT of State 1 in the Stroke group was negatively correlated with lower limb motor function scores and balance function, while the FT of State 3 was positively correlated with lower limb motor function scores and balance function, providing potential neuroimaging markers for clinical assessment.

The pathological oscillations occurring within the networkmay trigger the symptoms induced by the stroke, and stimulation of any node within the neural network could disrupt this pathological rhythm [65]. We propose that the interpretation of State 1 exhibits dual characteristics: Speciﬁcally, under pathological conditions, the persistent dominance of State 1 indeed reﬂects a loss of network integration capacity. Conversely, we suggest that rTMS (particularly dual-target stimulation) can disrupt the dynamic rhythms of brain networks, transforming the current state into a controllable stable state. It is conceivable that establishing new connections from this weakly connected state may be more feasible, laying the groundwork for greater network ﬂexibility [66].

It is important to note that the neural effects of the temporalstimulation paradigm employed in this study are complex. A key consideration is the potential inﬂuence of homeostatic plasticity. Homeostatic plasticity mechanisms ensure neuronal network excitability remains within physiological

bounds, with the history of prior synaptic activity modulating the direction and extent of plasticity induced by subsequent stimulation [67], [68]. In this study, the initial high-frequency rTMS applied to the L-DLPFC may have induced heightened excitability in this region and its associated networks. Given the functional and anatomical connectivity between the DLPFC and SMA, this alteration may have correspondingly modiﬁed the baseline excitability state of the SMA prior
10 IEEE TRANSACTIONS ON NEURAL SYSTEMS AND REHABILITATION ENGINEERING

to receiving stimulation. Consequently, the effects of the subsequent rTMS applied to the SMA may not represent a simple superposition but rather an optimized network response pattern, regulated by homeostatic plasticity, that differs from what would be observed with single-target stimulation alone.

Dual-target neuromodulation therapy is an emergingresearch direction in neuroscience [69]. A meta-analysis of 22 studies showed that compared to single-target stimulation, sequential dual-target stimulation can achieve higher efﬁcacy by enhancing neural network plasticity and improving functional connectivity across cognitive domains [16]. Additionally, high-frequency rTMS (HF-rTMS) applied in a sequential dual-target stimulation paradigm has been shown to enhance synaptic efﬁcacy, induce effects similar to long-term potentiation, and strengthen functional connectivity between brain regions [70], [71]. Similarly, in this study, HF-rTMS was sequentially applied to the L-DLPFC and SMA of Stroke with lower limb motor dysfunction, and it was found that the connectivity between M1_L, S1_L, and DLPFC_R, SFC_R varied to different degrees within different dFNC states. This suggests that the current study protocol may better reshape the nervous system by optimizing the cross-regional information integration patterns between the frontal-sensorimotor cortexmotor cortex loop in patients. The aforementioned mechanisms and results suggest that rTMS methods based on neural network regulation may promote brain functional remodeling in Stroke by enhancing synaptic plasticity and repairing damaged functional connections.

In summary, our study further validates that the therapeutic mechanisms of rTMS can inﬂuence dynamic functional connectivity between large-scale brain networks. Additionally, dynamic functional connectivity between brain networks can serve as a predictive indicator of rTMS treatment efﬁcacy. Finally, for Stroke with lower limb motor impairments, compared to traditional single-target stimulation, sequential dual-target stimulation may represent an efﬁcient therapeutic modality to promote brain remodeling.

Our results further suggest that not only the degree of modularity itself but also the dynamic transition ability between states may be key indicators of functional prognosis. Interestingly, while bilateral stimulation primarily affects State 1 in HC group, it also signiﬁcantly impacts the FT of State 2 in the Stroke group, a difference that may reﬂect the Stroke brain’s speciﬁc response pattern to neuromodulation. Additionally, our correlation analysis results showed that the FT of State 1 in the Stroke group was negatively correlated with lower limb motor function scores and balance function, while the FT of State 3 was positively correlated with lower limb motor function scores and balance function, providing potential neuroimaging markers for clinical assessment.

The pathological oscillations occurring within the networkmay trigger the symptoms induced by the stroke, and stimulation of any node within the neural network could disrupt this pathological rhythm [65]. We propose that the interpretation of State 1 exhibits dual characteristics: Speciﬁcally, under pathological conditions, the persistent dominance of State 1 indeed reﬂects a loss of network integration capacity. Conversely, we suggest that rTMS (particularly dual-target stimulation) can disrupt the dynamic rhythms of brain networks, transforming the current state into a controllable stable state. It is conceivable that establishing new connections from this weakly connected state may be more feasible, laying the groundwork for greater network ﬂexibility [66].

In this study, the initial high-frequency rTMS applied to the L-DLPFC may have induced heightened excitability in this region and its associated networks. Given the functional and anatomical connectivity between the DLPFC and SMA, this alteration may have correspondingly modiﬁed the baseline excitability state of the SMA prior

Consequently, the effects of the subsequent rTMS applied to the SMA may not represent a simple superposition but rather an optimized network response pattern, regulated by homeostatic plasticity, that differs from what would be observed with single-target stimulation alone.

Dual-target neuromodulation therapy is an emergingresearch direction in neuroscience [69]. A meta-analysis of 22 studies showed that compared to single-target stimulation, sequential dual-target stimulation can achieve higher efﬁcacy by enhancing neural network plasticity and improving functional connectivity across cognitive domains [16]. Additionally, high-frequency rTMS (HF-rTMS) applied in a sequential dual-target stimulation paradigm has been shown to enhance synaptic efﬁcacy, induce effects similar to long-term potentiation, and strengthen functional connectivity between brain regions [70], [71]. Similarly, in this study, HF-rTMS was sequentially applied to the L-DLPFC and SMA of Stroke with lower limb motor dysfunction, and it was found that the connectivity between M1_L, S1_L, and DLPFC_R, SFC_R varied to different degrees within different dFNC states. This suggests that the current study protocol may better reshape the nervous system by optimizing the cross-regional information integration patterns between the frontal-sensorimotor cortexmotor cortex loop in patients. The aforementioned mechanisms and results suggest that rTMS methods based on neural network regulation may promote brain functional remodeling in Stroke by enhancing synaptic plasticity and repairing damaged functional connections.

In summary, our study further validates that the therapeutic mechanisms of rTMS can inﬂuence dynamic functional connectivity between large-scale brain networks. Additionally, dynamic functional connectivity between brain networks can serve as a predictive indicator of rTMS treatment efﬁcacy. Finally, for Stroke with lower limb motor impairments, compared to traditional single-target stimulation, sequential dual-target stimulation may represent an efﬁcient therapeutic modality to promote brain remodeling.
Limitations

Our study also has some limitations. First, a potential limitation of this study is the absence of a sham-rTMS control group. Future experimental designs should include a sham-rTMS group as a control to better understand the effects of different stimulation patterns on dynamic brain functional networks. Second, the selection of sliding window size may inﬂuence the assessment of dynamic brain connectivity. Future analyses should be conducted using different window widths to validate the reliability and reproducibility of the results. Third, the 48hour washout period may have been too short to completely avoid carryover effects between experimental sessions. Fourth, the localization of stimulation targets (L-DLPFC and SMA) in this study relied on EEG caps based on the international 10-20 system rather than individualized MRI navigation. This may introduce some degree of inter-individual variability. Future studies employing individualized neuro-navigation will enhance the precision of target localization. Finally, a key limitation of this study is the absence of resting-state fNIRS measurements following rTMS intervention. Consequently, our ﬁndings capture only the immediate online effects of stimulation, without clarifying whether the observed dynamic functional network connectivity changes (e.g., increased FT in state 1) persist as a lasting aftereffect into the poststimulation phase. Future studies should incorporate longer post-intervention monitoring periods to elucidate the temporal dynamics and potential enduring beneﬁts of sequential dualtarget TMS.
